object.title: Laboratory geometry: a restricted inertial chart, its spatial slices and fixed-time fields
object.statement:
Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame with inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$ ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), let $c>0$ be the framework's conversion constant, and let $\delta$ be the Euclidean spatial form of that frame on $n^\perp$, $n:=e_0$, with norm $|\cdot|$ and positive spatial orientation ([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]). Fix a nonempty open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]) and a nonempty open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, and put

$$U:=\{p\in A:\ \text{there are }t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\text{ with }x^0(p)=ct,\ (x^1,x^2,x^3)(p)=y\}.$$

Then: (a) [Chart restriction] $x(U)=\{(ct,y):t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\}$ and $\Phi:U\to I\times\Omega$, $\Phi(p):=(x^0(p)/c,(x^1,x^2,x^3)(p))$, is a bijection, because the inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$ is a bijection and $c>0$; its components are the laboratory time coordinate $t(p):=x^0(p)/c$ and the laboratory position $r(p):=(x^1(p),x^2(p),x^3(p))$. (b) [Slices and spatial structure] For each $t\in I$ the slice $U_t:=\{p\in U:t(p)=t\}$ is carried bijectively onto $\Omega$ by $r$; the constant vector $n=e_0$ is future unit timelike, and $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is the $\delta$-orthonormal positively oriented basis of $n^\perp$ in which the coordinates of $r$ are expressed. (c) [Laboratory fields] A laboratory field of rank $m$ is a map $F:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^m$; it is identified with the map $U\to\mathbb R^m$, $p\mapsto F(r(p),t(p))$, and with the family $(F(\cdot,t))_{t\in I}$ of maps $\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$, its values at fixed time. Such a field is of class $C^k$ when the map $(y,t)\mapsto F(y,t)$ is $C^k$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; then $\partial_{y_i}F$ (at fixed $t$) and $\partial_tF$ (at fixed $y$) are the partial derivatives of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. No regularity of a field is asserted beyond the class stated for it. (d) [Conventions] The product decomposition is a coordinate identification inside the single inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$; it is not a Galilean transformation, it does not compare two inertial frames, and it does not assert absolute simultaneity. The objects $I,\Omega,t,r,\delta$ and the identification $\mathbb R^3\cong n^\perp$ belong to the named frame; changes of inertial description are the proper orthochronous maps adopted in [[post-sr-inertial-covariance]]. The frame is an origin together with an ordered basis; it is not a congruence of observers, and no moving observer field is defined here.
object.strategy: A construction definition with elementary verifications. The inertial chart $x$ of [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]] is a bijection, so its restriction to the set of events whose chart coordinates lie in $cI\times\Omega$ has image $cI\times\Omega$; composing with the bijection $cI\times\Omega\to I\times\Omega$, $(ct,y)\mapsto(t,y)$ (bijective because $c>0$) gives the bijection $\Phi$. Each slice $U_t$ is $\Phi^{-1}(\{t\}\times\Omega)$, on which $r$ restricts to a bijection onto $\Omega$. The claims about $n$, $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$, $\delta$ and the orientation are exactly the content of [[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]; the $C^k$ notion is that of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]] and the two kinds of partial derivative are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]] applied to the product coordinates. Clause (d) records conventions only: the frame dependence of $r,\delta$ and slices is stated rather than hidden, and no Galilean or observer-congruence claim is made. Nothing here uses a theorem of the framework, and the laboratory region may be a proper subset of $A$; no global chart of $A$ other than the given inertial chart is asserted.

object.title: Polarization, magnetization, bound and free sources, and the fields D and H
object.statement:
Let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$, its frame basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$, its units, its fields $E,B$ and its source densities $\rho,J$ be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-si-conventions]], [[def-em-fields]] and [[def-em-sources]], and let the averaging convention be that of [[post-em-coarse-graining]], in whose sense the objects below are macroscopic. Any convolution used to instantiate that reading is taken on its declared exact interior-footprint domain, or under a declared locally integrable compatible extension covering every used footprint. Its every-time use requires every-time locally integrable spatial slices; joint spacetime local integrability alone supplies only the almost-every-time branch. The joint C2 regularity specified below is a separate model hypothesis, not a consequence of spatial smoothing.
(a) [Polarization and magnetization] The material model specifies two maps $P,M:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^2$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]] on the open set $\Omega\times I$: $P$ is the electric dipole moment per unit volume, in $\mathrm C\,\mathrm m^{-2}$, and $M$ the magnetic dipole moment per unit volume, in $\mathrm A\,\mathrm m^{-1}$, both read in the frame basis. They are data of the chosen material model: this definition does not compute them from $E$ and $B$, and no relation between $(P,M)$ and the fields is asserted here.
(b) [Bound sources] Write $\operatorname{div}$ and $\operatorname{curl}$ for the divergence and curl of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] taken at fixed $t$, and $\partial_t$ for the partial derivative of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]] at fixed position, and define the bound charge density and bound current density by $$\rho_b:=-\operatorname{div}P,\qquad J_b:=\partial_tP+\operatorname{curl}M.$$ Since $P,M$ are jointly $C^2$, $\rho_b$ and $J_b$ are continuous (indeed $C^1$); $\rho_b$ carries $\mathrm C\,\mathrm m^{-3}$ and $J_b$ carries $\mathrm A\,\mathrm m^{-2}$.
(c) [Free sources] Define $\rho_f:=\rho-\rho_b$ and $J_f:=J-J_b$, in the same units as $\rho$ and $J$; these are the free charge and free current densities of the model. The decomposition $\rho=\rho_f+\rho_b$, $J=J_f+J_b$ is part of the chosen material model: the same total pair $(\rho,J)$ with a different pair $(P,M)$ is a different model.
(d) [Displacement and magnetic intensity] Define the electric displacement and the magnetic intensity by $$D:=\varepsilon_0E+P,\qquad H:=\mu_0^{-1}B-M,$$ where $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and $\mu_0,c>0$ are the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]]; $D$ carries $\mathrm C\,\mathrm m^{-2}$ and $H$ carries $\mathrm A\,\mathrm m^{-1}$.
(e) [Status] This item fixes objects and the bound/free convention only. No field equation ([[pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell]]), no constitutive relation ([[post-em-material-closure]]), no conservation of the bound pair ([[pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell]](a)) and no identification of $P,M$ with microscopic dipole sums is asserted here.
object.strategy: An explicit type/domain/convention definition. The regions, fields and sources are those of the named suppliers; the derivatives in (b) are the published divergence, curl and partial derivative; the constants and units are those of [[def-em-si-conventions]]; the $C^2$ class is that of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; the macroscopic reading is the convention of [[post-em-coarse-graining]], with its actual footprint/compatible-extension and slice hypotheses carried whenever convolution is used. Joint C2 regularity of the model maps is assumed separately; the spatial averaging operation proves neither time differentiability nor the existence of microscopic dipole sums. The definition records explicitly that $(P,M)$ are model data read in the laboratory frame basis, that the bound/free split is a modelling choice, and that no constitutive relation between $(P,M)$ and $(E,B)$ is included. Well-definedness of $\rho_b,J_b$ as continuous fields is the componentwise sum/product differentiability calculus of [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]. No field equation, no derivative of the physical fields and no microscopic interpretation is used.

object.title: Framework-local SI units, the vacuum constants and the exact/measured status of their values
object.statement: Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]. (a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$ carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant $\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of $\mu_0$ is asserted (the pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical estimate/uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$ or a current measured value); the electric constant is defined within the framework by $\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$, so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$. (b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the charge density $\rho$ of [[def-em-sources]] carries C m$^{-3}$ and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where $1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$ carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic two-form of [[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]] carry T; a force carries the newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$. (c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram (kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ carries kg m s$^{-1}$ ([[post-sr-massive-particle-dynamics]]); field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$. (d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI, they do not by themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light, which is the physical adoption of [[post-em-minkowski-physical-model]].
object.strategy: A convention definition: it fixes the coordinate normalisation $x^0=ct$, the unit of each quantity used in this framework, the exact SI defining values of $c$ and $e$ and the measured status of $\mu_0$. The exact values $c=299\,792\,458$ m/s and $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}$ C, and the statements that the new definition of the ampere fixes $e$ rather than $\mu_0$, that $\mu_0$ must now be determined experimentally, and that $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$ remains exact, are taken from the SI brochure's defining-constants table and its ampere section. The framework's definition of $\varepsilon_0$ by $(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ is a definition consistent with that exact relation; the uncertainty carried by $\varepsilon_0$ is recorded rather than hidden. The dimensional checks of the framework's equations and couplings are developed on the companion examples page of this pair. No exact or current measured numerical value of $\mu_0$ is asserted and no experiment is claimed. The historical nominal and adoption uncertainty are explicitly source context, not a substitution for the current experimentally determined constant.

supplier_snapshots.actual_public_statement:
Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

## Definition

and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and

3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.

   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so

   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

## Remarks

- **Scope: the concrete form only.** What is defined above is the Euclidean inner
  product on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ and nothing more. The general theory of inner
  product spaces — abstract inner products, orthonormal bases, Gram-Schmidt,
  orthogonal projection and orthogonal complements of arbitrary subspaces — is
  planned for a page of this library that comes **earlier in the plan order** and
  is not yet built. No item on this page claims anything about abstract inner
  product spaces, and no item on this page introduces the general notion.

- **The standard basis and coordinates.** For $i < n$ the standard unit vector
  $e_i \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ has $e_i(i) = 1$ and $e_i(j) = 0$ for $j \ne i$
  ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). Then $\langle x, e_i\rangle = x_i$: the list
  $k \mapsto x_k (e_i)_k$ vanishes except at $k = i$, where its value is $x_i$,
  and a list vanishing off one index sums to its value there
  ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 3, splitting the range at $i$). So the
  coordinates of $x$ are recovered by testing against the standard basis, which
  is the form used repeatedly below.

## Statement

Complex conjugation is a real-field automorphism satisfying
$$\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w,\qquad \overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w,\qquad \overline{\overline z}=z.$$
For every $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$z\overline z=|z|^2,\qquad |z|\ge0,\qquad |z|=0\Longleftrightarrow z=0,$$
$$|zw|=|z||w|,\qquad |z+w|\le |z|+|w|.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $z=a+bi$ and $w=u+vi$.

[F1] Complex numbers have unique real coordinates and the coordinate addition and multiplication formulas ([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]).

[F2] Conjugation and modulus are defined by $\overline{a+bi}=a-bi$ and $|a+bi|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$ ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]).

[F3] The real numbers are a complete ordered field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]), and every nonnegative element of a complete ordered field has a unique nonnegative square root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

[F4] For nonnegative elements $r,s$ of an ordered field, $r\le s$ if and only if $r^2\le s^2$ ([[lem-of-square-monotone]]).

[F5] The square of every nonzero element of an ordered field is positive ([[lem-of-square-positive]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Coordinate expansion using [F1] and [F2] proves the two homomorphism laws, that conjugation fixes every real number, and that applying it twice is the identity. Thus conjugation is an involutive real-field automorphism. [F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 Direct multiplication gives $z\overline z=a^2+b^2=|z|^2$. [F1, F2, algebra]

1.3 Lagrange's identity gives $$ (a^2+b^2)(u^2+v^2)-(au+bv)^2=(av-bu)^2\ge0. $$ The final inequality follows from [F5], with the zero case included. [F5, algebra]

2.1 By [F2] and [F3], $|z|\ge0$. If $z=0$, then $|z|=0$; conversely, $|z|=0$ makes $a^2+b^2=0$, and [F5] forces $a=b=0$. [F2, F3, F5, step 1.2]

3.1 Apply step 1.2 to $zw$ and use step 1.1: $|zw|^2=(zw)\overline{zw}=(z\overline z)(w\overline w) =|z|^2|w|^2$. Both sides of $|zw|=|z||w|$ are nonnegative, so uniqueness in [F3] proves multiplicativity. [F3, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1]

3.2 Hence $au+bv\le |z||w|$: if $au+bv\le0$ this follows from $|z||w|\ge0$; otherwise both quantities are nonnegative, step 1.3 and [F4] give the inequality after squaring. [F4, step 2.1, step 1.3]

4.1 Expanding with [F1] and [F2], then using step 3.2, gives $$ |z+w|^2=a^2+b^2+u^2+v^2+2(au+bv) \le (|z|+|w|)^2. $$ [F1, F2, step 1.2, step 3.2, algebra]

5.1 Both sides of $|z+w|\le|z|+|w|$ are nonnegative, so [F4] turns the squared inequality in step 4.1 into the triangle inequality. [F4, step 2.1, step 4.1] ∎

## Statement

For all $u,v,w\in\mathbb R^3$, the cross product is bilinear and alternating, $\langle u\times v,w\rangle=\det[u\ v\ w]$, and $u\times v$ is orthogonal to both $u$ and $v$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Vectors $u,v,w\in\mathbb R^3$ and a scalar $c\in\mathbb R$.

[L1] The cross product is given by its three coordinate differences of products ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]]), and the Euclidean inner product is the coordinate dot product ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

[L2] The determinant of a real $3\times3$ matrix is its signed permutation sum ([[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Substitution in [L1] gives $(u+u')\times v=u\times v+u'\times v$, $(cu)\times v=c(u\times v)$, and the corresponding two identities in the second argument. [L1, algebra]

1.2 The same coordinate formula gives $u\times u=0$ and $v\times u=-(u\times v)$, so the product is alternating. [L1, algebra]

1.3 Expanding the dot product in [L1] yields $\langle u\times v,w\rangle=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y)w_x+(u_zv_x-u_xv_z)w_y+(u_xv_y-u_yv_x)w_z$, which is the determinant $\det[u\ v\ w]$ by [L2]. [L1, L2, algebra]

2.1 Taking $w=u$ or $w=v$ makes the determinant have two equal columns and hence zero; therefore $u\times v$ is orthogonal to both factors. The calculation includes zero and parallel vectors. [step 1.3, L2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) with positive cone $P$, and
let $a, b, c \in F$.

1. If $a > 0$ and $b > 0$ then $ab > 0$.
2. If $a > 0$ and $b < 0$ then $ab < 0$.
3. If $a < 0$ and $b < 0$ then $ab > 0$.
4. If $c > 0$ then $a < b \iff ac < bc$.
5. If $c < 0$ then $a < b \iff bc < ac$ (multiplication by a negative reverses order).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An ordered field $F$ with positive cone $P$, and elements $a, b, c \in F$.

[L1] For $x, y \in F$: $x < y \iff y - x \in P$; $x > 0 \iff x \in P$; $x < 0 \iff -x \in P$; and (trichotomy) for each $x$ exactly one of $x \in P$, $x = 0$, $-x \in P$ holds, so $0 \notin P$ and $x \in P \Rightarrow x \neq 0$ ([[def-ordered-field]]).

[L2] $P$ is closed under multiplication: if $u, v \in P$ then $uv \in P$ (axiom O2 of [[def-ordered-field]]).

[L3] In any field, $(-u)v = -(uv)$ and $(-u)(-v) = uv$ ([[lem-of-mult-neg]]).

[L4] In any field, $0 \cdot u = 0$ ([[lem-of-zero-mult]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Assume $a > 0$ and $b > 0$, i.e. $a \in P$ and $b \in P$; closure gives $ab \in P$, so $ab > 0$, proving claim 1. [assume-hyp, L1, L2]

1.2 Assume $a > 0$ and $b < 0$, i.e. $a \in P$ and $-b \in P$; closure gives $a(-b) \in P$. [assume-hyp, L1, L2]

1.3 Assume $a < 0$ and $b < 0$, i.e. $-a \in P$ and $-b \in P$; closure gives $(-a)(-b) \in P$. [assume-hyp, L1, L2]

1.4 Assume $c > 0$ and $a < b$, i.e. $c \in P$ and $b - a \in P$; closure gives $(b - a)c \in P$. [assume-hyp, L1, L2]

1.5 Assume $c < 0$ and $a < b$, i.e. $-c \in P$ and $b - a \in P$; closure gives $(b - a)(-c) \in P$. [assume-hyp, L1, L2]

2.1 Since $a(-b) = -(ab)$ by L3, step 1.2 gives $-(ab) \in P$, so $ab < 0$, proving claim 2. [step 1.2, L3, L1]

2.2 Since $(-a)(-b) = ab$ by L3, step 1.3 gives $ab \in P$, so $ab > 0$, proving claim 3. [step 1.3, L3, L1]

2.3 By distributivity $(b - a)c = bc - ac$, so step 1.4 gives $bc - ac \in P$, i.e. $ac < bc$: this is the forward direction of claim 4. [step 1.4, algebra, L1]

2.4 By L3 and distributivity $(b - a)(-c) = -((b - a)c) = -(bc - ac) = ac - bc$, so step 1.5 gives $ac - bc \in P$, i.e. $bc < ac$: this is the forward direction of claim 5. [step 1.5, L3, algebra, L1]

3.1 Conversely, assume $c > 0$ and $ac < bc$; by trichotomy exactly one of $a < b$, $a = b$, $b < a$ holds. If $a = b$ then $ac = bc$, contradicting $ac < bc$; if $b < a$ then the argument of step 2.3 applied to the pair $b < a$ gives $bc < ac$, so $bc - ac \in P$ (from $ac < bc$) while $ac - bc \in P$ (from $bc < ac$), putting the element $bc - ac$ and its negative $ac - bc$ both in $P$, which trichotomy forbids; hence $a < b$: this completes claim 4. [assume-hyp, step 2.3, L4, L1, algebra]

4.1 Conversely, assume $c < 0$ and $bc < ac$; by trichotomy exactly one of $a < b$, $a = b$, $b < a$ holds. If $a = b$ then $ac = bc$, contradicting $bc < ac$; if $b < a$ then the argument of step 2.4 applied to the pair $b < a$ gives $ac < bc$, so $ac - bc \in P$ (from $bc < ac$) while $bc - ac \in P$ (from $ac < bc$), putting the element $ac - bc$ and its negative $bc - ac$ both in $P$, which trichotomy forbids; hence $a < b$: this completes claim 5. [assume-hyp, step 2.4, L4, L1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $F$ be an ordered field. For $a, b \ge 0$:

$$a < b \iff a^2 < b^2, \qquad a \le b \iff a^2 \le b^2.$$

More generally, for arbitrary $a, b \in F$, $a^2 < b^2 \iff |a| < |b|$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Elements $a, b$ of an ordered field $F$.

[L1] For a positive factor $s > 0$ and any $t$: $t > 0 \iff st > 0$; this is [[lem-of-sign-rules]] (the rule $c > 0 \Rightarrow (x < y \iff xc < yc)$ taken at $x = 0$, $y = t$, $c = s$, using $0 \cdot s = 0$, [[lem-of-zero-mult]]).

[L2] Trichotomy: for $a, b$ exactly one of $a < b$, $a = b$, $a > b$ holds; and a sum of two nonnegatives with at least one positive is positive ([[def-ordered-field]]).

[L3] $|x| \ge 0$ and $|x|^2 = x^2$ for every $x$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The difference factors as $b^2 - a^2 = (b - a)(b + a)$. [algebra]

2.1 If $a, b \ge 0$ and $a < b$, then $b > 0$, so $b + a > 0$ by [L2], and $b - a > 0$; by [L1] with $s = b + a$ and $t = b - a$, $(b - a)(b + a) > 0$, i.e. $a^2 < b^2$. [L1, L2, step 1.1]

2.2 If $a, b \ge 0$ and $a^2 < b^2$, then $b^2 - a^2 > 0$, so $a, b$ are not both zero and $b + a > 0$ by [L2]; by [L1] with $s = b + a$, from $(b - a)(b + a) = b^2 - a^2 > 0$ we get $b - a > 0$, i.e. $a < b$. [L1, L2, step 1.1]

3.1 Hence for $a, b \ge 0$, $a < b \iff a^2 < b^2$. [step 2.1, step 2.2]

4.1 The $\le$ form follows by trichotomy: for $a, b \ge 0$, applying step 3.1 to the nonnegatives $b, a$ gives $a \le b \iff \lnot(b < a) \iff \lnot(b^2 < a^2) \iff a^2 \le b^2$. [step 3.1, L2]

5.1 For arbitrary $a, b$, [L3] gives $|a|, |b| \ge 0$ with $|a|^2 = a^2$ and $|b|^2 = b^2$; applying step 3.1 to $|a|, |b|$ yields $a^2 < b^2 \iff |a|^2 < |b|^2 \iff |a| < |b|$. [step 3.1, L3] ∎

object.title: Declared material-closure branches: linear nondispersive Ohmic response and the causal memory branch
object.statement:
Adopt as a modelling postulate of this framework the following constitutive branches for the material described by the macroscopic fields of [[def-em-polarization-magnetization]].
(a) [Material rest frame] The relations below are stated in a material rest frame: an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the Minkowski model of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]) in which the material element under consideration is at rest, with spatial basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$; when the material is at rest in the laboratory frame of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], the components below are the laboratory components. Boosting the material changes both the fields and the rest observer; this postulate does not assert that the relations below hold with the same constants in every frame.
(b) [Elementary inertial-rest branch] In the rest frame, with constant symmetric positive-definite matrices $\varepsilon,\mu\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ (the isotropic scalar cases $\varepsilon=\varepsilon\mathbf 1$, $\mu=\mu\mathbf 1$ with $\varepsilon,\mu>0$ included), the model takes $$D=\varepsilon E,\qquad B=\mu H,\qquad J_c=\sigma E,$$ where $\sigma\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ is symmetric positive semidefinite and $J_c$ is the conduction part of the free current, $J_f=J_c+J_{\mathrm{ext}}$ for a declared external free current $J_{\mathrm{ext}}$; local, linear and nondispersive (instantaneous) response is part of this restricted assumption. In the isotropic case an exact broadband interpretation of the constant-coefficient law additionally requires $\varepsilon\mu\ge c^{-2}$, so that the characteristic speed $1/\sqrt{\varepsilon\mu}$ does not exceed the vacuum speed $c$; without that condition, and in the anisotropic branch, the constant-coefficient law is a declared finite-band effective phase-response model and carries no universal front-speed claim.
(c) [Causal memory branch] Alternatively, and again in the rest frame, the polarisation response to the electric history is the causal convolution $$P(t)=\varepsilon_0\int_0^\infty K(s)\,E(t-s)\,ds$$ for a declared real matrix kernel $K:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ in $L^1(0,\infty)$ ([[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]); the integral then converges absolutely for bounded continuous histories $E$ because $|K_{jk}(s)E_k(t-s)|\le(\sup|E_k|)|K_{jk}(s)|$. The kernel class actually used, together with causality and passivity, is part of the model and is analysed in [[pthm-em-causal-dispersive-response]]; neither causality nor passivity is automatic. A finitely-subtracted analytic response may instead be declared by a scalar transfer function $\chi$ that is holomorphic on the open upper half-plane, of class $C^1$ on the real boundary away from a real subtraction point $\omega_0$, holomorphic on a neighbourhood of $\omega_0$, and satisfies $|\chi(z)|\le C(1+|z|^{n-1})$ on $\{\operatorname{Im}z\ge0\}$ outside a compact set for some integer $n\ge1$ and constant $C>0$ ([[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]).
(d) [Status] These are adopted model assumptions, one branch at a time; the framework does not derive them from the vacuum equations or from coarse graining, and no microscopic mechanism, material data or empirical validity is claimed. Ferroelectric and ferromagnetic response, hysteresis, nonlinear response and general nonlocal response lie outside the branches declared here.
object.strategy: An adopted nonproof formulation. The objects are those of [[def-em-polarization-magnetization]]; the macroscopic field equations whose formulation the closure completes are those of [[pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell]]; the rest-frame notion is the inertial frame of [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]] used by [[def-em-lab-geometry]], and the memory-branch kernel class is the $L^1$ notion of [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]], whose absolute convergence for bounded continuous histories is the elementary domination displayed in the statement. The finitely-subtracted branch uses the holomorphy notion of [[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]] and states its growth and boundary hypotheses explicitly rather than hiding them. Clause (d) records that the branches are assumptions with no microscopic or empirical content. No proof is supplied and none is claimed, in accordance with the nonproof status of a postulate; the source and scope review covers the formulation, the rest-frame and scale qualifications and the non-derivation.

## Statement

Let $F$ be an ordered field. If $0 < a < b$ and $0 < c < d$ then $ac < bd$. If $0 \le a \le b$ and $0 \le c \le d$ then $ac \le bd$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Elements $a, b, c, d$ of an ordered field $F$.

[L1] For a positive multiplier $c > 0$: $x < y \iff xc < yc$; multiplying a strict inequality by a positive element preserves it ([[lem-of-sign-rules]]).

[L2] For $c \ge 0$: $x \le y \Rightarrow xc \le yc$; the case $c > 0$ is [L1] and the case $c = 0$ gives $0 \le 0$ ([[lem-of-sign-rules]]).

[L3] The order is transitive: if $x < y$ and $y < z$ then $x < z$, and likewise for $\le$, since the positive cone is closed under addition ([[def-ordered-field]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Assume $0 < a < b$ and $0 < c < d$; since $c > 0$, scaling $a < b$ by $c$ gives $ac < bc$. [L1]

1.2 Since $b > 0$ (from $0 < a < b$), scaling $c < d$ by $b$ gives $bc < bd$. [L1]

1.3 Assume instead $0 \le a \le b$ and $0 \le c \le d$; since $c \ge 0$, from $a \le b$ we get $ac \le bc$. [L2]

1.4 Since $b \ge 0$ (from $0 \le a \le b$), from $c \le d$ we get $bc \le bd$. [L2]

2.1 By transitivity, $ac < bc < bd$, hence $ac < bd$, proving the strict claim. [L3, step 1.1, step 1.2]

2.2 By transitivity of $\le$, $ac \le bc \le bd$, hence $ac \le bd$, proving the nonstrict claim. [L3, step 1.3, step 1.4]

3.1 Both the strict and the nonstrict inequalities hold. [step 2.1, step 2.2] ∎

object.title: The macroscopic Maxwell equations in terms of D, H and the free sources
object.statement:
Assume the smooth branch of the vacuum Maxwell postulate [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] on the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]: fields $E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ jointly of class $C^1$ with the additional derivatives required by each equation existing and continuous, and continuous source densities $\rho,J$ of [[def-em-sources]]. Let $P,M$ and the derived objects $\rho_b,J_b,\rho_f,J_f,D,H$ be those of [[def-em-polarization-magnetization]], with $P,M$ of class $C^2$, and use the operators of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. Then:
(a) [Bound-source conservation] $\partial_t\rho_b+\operatorname{div}J_b=0$ on $\Omega\times I$. Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the regular-distribution and classical-compatibility interfaces below. Identify continuous sources with their regular distributions using [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]] and [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]. Then $$\partial_t\rho_f+\operatorname{div}J_f=\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J$$ as distributions on $U$, with derivatives as in [[def-distributional-derivative]]: the free pair is distributionally conserved exactly when the total pair is. Under the adopted four vacuum equations both sides are zero distributions, by [[thm-distributional-differentiation-is-continuous-and-commutes]]. These statements do not require classical derivatives of $\rho,J$. Where the partial derivatives $\partial_t\rho$ and $\partial_{x_i}J_i$ exist, the same identity holds pointwise by differentiating the free/bound decomposition; in particular, if these derivatives are continuous on $U$, both pairs satisfy the classical pointwise continuity equation. The bound-source conservation equation remains classical and uses only $P,M\in C^2$.
(b) [Macroscopic equations] On $\Omega\times I$, $$\operatorname{div}D=\rho_f,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}H=J_f+\partial_tD.$$
(c) [Interpretation and scope] Equations (b) are an exact rewriting of the adopted vacuum equations under the decomposition of [[def-em-polarization-magnetization]]: the two equations written in $E$ and $B$ are unchanged, and the $D$ and $H$ equations hold for every $C^2$ pair $(P,M)$, independently of any constitutive law. The classical bound identity of (a) uses the exchange of $\partial_t$ with $\operatorname{div}$ for $C^2$ data; the free/total identity is distributional in the stated continuous-source class, with its classical interpretation only under the additional derivatives stated in (a). The distributional conservation conclusion embeds the adopted smooth solution only; no macroscopic field-equation claim is made for the weak branch of the Maxwell postulate, for singular or sheet sources or for discontinuous $(P,M)$; no constitutive relation and no empirical statement is made.
object.strategy: **Proof technique:** direct substitution, componentwise. (a): from [[def-em-polarization-magnetization]](b), $\operatorname{div}J_b=\operatorname{div}\partial_tP+\operatorname{div}\operatorname{curl}M$. The second term vanishes: in components $\operatorname{div}\operatorname{curl}M=\sum_{i,j,k=1}^3\epsilon_{ijk}\partial_i\partial_jM_k$, and pairwise cancellation of the mixed partials $\partial_i\partial_jM_k=\partial_j\partial_iM_k$ is [[thm-clairaut-schwarz-mixed-partials]] applied to the $C^2$ components of $M$; the first term equals $\partial_t\operatorname{div}P$ by the same theorem applied to the $C^2$ components of $P$; adding $-\partial_t\operatorname{div}P$ gives zero. Linearity of $\partial_t$, $\operatorname{div}$ and $\operatorname{curl}$ is [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]] read componentwise. (b): Gauss's law $\operatorname{div}E=(\rho_f+\rho_b)/\varepsilon_0$ together with $\rho_b=-\operatorname{div}P$ gives $\operatorname{div}(\varepsilon_0E+P)=\rho_f$, i.e. $\operatorname{div}D=\rho_f$. The equations $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$ are unchanged. Ampere's law $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$ with $J=J_f+\partial_tP+\operatorname{curl}M$ gives, after dividing by $\mu_0$ and moving $\operatorname{curl}M$ to the left, $\operatorname{curl}(\mu_0^{-1}B-M)=J_f+\partial_tP+\varepsilon_0\partial_tE$, where $(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}=\varepsilon_0$; the right-hand side is $J_f+\partial_t(\varepsilon_0E+P)=J_f+\partial_tD$, so $\operatorname{curl}H=J_f+\partial_tD$. (c) records the scope: the identities are conditional on the adopted postulates and on $P,M\in C^2$; no constitutive content is used. For the free/total identity, subtract the regular distributions of the classical bound pair from those of the continuous total pair and differentiate linearly. Under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, [[thm-distributional-differentiation-is-continuous-and-commutes]] identifies the $C^1$ bound derivatives with their classical regular distributions, so their sum is zero; this proves the distributional identity without differentiating the merely continuous total sources classically. Embed the four adopted $C^1$ Maxwell equations and apply spatial divergence to Ampere: commuting distributional derivatives cancels $\operatorname{div}\operatorname{curl}B$ and Gauss gives $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$. If the displayed source derivatives exist, linearity gives the pointwise free/total identity; if they are continuous, classical compatibility and injectivity of the regular-distribution embedding give pointwise zero. Only the regular-distribution/classical-compatibility branch invokes $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$; the classical bound calculation and the macroscopic substitution in (b) remain choice-free.

object.title: Stationary macroscopic interface jump conditions for D, B, E and H
object.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), the hypothesis under which [[lem-em-interface-derivatives]] and the surface conventions of [[def-em-weak-sources]] are stated, and let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]].
Let $S\subset\Omega$ be a fixed compact embedded $C^2$ hypersurface with a chosen unit normal $n$ pointing from the side $\Omega_-$ to the side $\Omega_+$ ([[def-em-surface-distribution]]), let $\sigma_f:S\times I\to\mathbb R$ and $K_f:S\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous with $K_f(x,t)\cdot n(x)=0$ for all $(x,t)$ (a free surface charge density and a tangential free surface current density, both stationary in $t$), and let $\rho_v:(\Omega\setminus S)\times I\to\mathbb R$ and $J_v:(\Omega\setminus S)\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous and locally integrable on $\Omega\times I$. Let $E,B,D,H:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be locally integrable on $\Omega\times I$ and of class $C^1$ on $(\Omega\setminus S)\times I$, with the joint one-sided $C^1$ extension property: around every $(x_0,t_0)\in S\times I$, each side of each field is the restriction of a $C^1$ function on an open spacetime neighbourhood of the corresponding closed side of a smaller stationary graph cylinder, so that the fields and their first space and time derivatives extend continuously to that side, locally uniformly on compact cylinders. Write $[F]=F_+-F_-$ for the jump of the one-sided traces.
[Thin-interface hypothesis] Suppose that $E,B,D,H$ satisfy the four macroscopic equations of [[pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell]] in the distributional sense on $U$ with the source pair $\rho_f=\rho_v+\sigma_f\delta_S$, $J_f=J_v+K_f\delta_S$, where the stationary-sheet pairings are those of [[def-em-weak-sources]](c) and the equations are $\operatorname{div}D=\rho_f$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$, $\operatorname{curl}H=J_f+\partial_tD$ as identities in the sense of [[def-distribution]], the fields being identified with their regular distributions ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]) and $\psi$ ranging over $C_c^\infty(U)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]], [[def-distributional-derivative]]). This thin-interface solution hypothesis is a modelling assumption of the statement: it is the natural weakening of the smooth macroscopic equations to fields with a common stationary discontinuity, and it is not deduced from the smooth-region equations alone.
Then, pointwise on $S\times I$, $$n\cdot[D]=\sigma_f,\qquad n\cdot[B]=0,\qquad n\times[E]=0,\qquad n\times[H]=K_f,$$ with the Euclidean inner and cross products of the one-sided traces ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]); equivalently $\sigma_f=n\cdot[D]$ and $K_f=n\times[H]$ recover the free sheet densities from the field jumps.
[Weak-trace branch] If instead of the joint extension hypothesis the fields have the original one-sided spatial $C^1$ extensions at each time and, in addition, the piecewise first spatial and temporal derivatives are in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$ and the one-sided field traces are measurable and locally integrable on $S\times I$ with respect to $dS\,dt$, then the same four identities hold as identities of sheet distributions and for $dS\,dt$-almost every $(x,t)$; since the traces are spatially continuous at each fixed time, they hold for every $x\in S$ for almost every $t$, and at every $(x,t)$ whenever the jump densities are additionally jointly continuous. Merely having one-sided spatial $C^1$ traces separately at every time does not justify the last upgrade.
[Scope] In the joint one-sided spacetime $C^1$ extension branch, stationarity and the joint extensions make $\partial_tD$ and $\partial_tB$ locally bounded near $S$ and hence locally integrable, contributing no delta terms. In the weak-trace branch the explicitly assumed locally integrable temporal derivatives provide this conclusion instead. No magnetic charge and no magnetic surface current are present in the sources; no dipolar sheet layer (a concentrated dipole distribution in $P$ or $M$, which would make the fields non-integrable) is included. No existence theorem for fields with singular sources is asserted, no constitutive law is used, and no empirical claim is made.
object.strategy: **Proof technique:** apply [[lem-em-interface-derivatives]] to the four fields and match the coefficients of the surface distribution. By [[lem-em-interface-derivatives]] ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ declared), for $C^1$-off-$S$ fields with one-sided $C^1$ traces, $\operatorname{div}D=\{\operatorname{div}D\}_{\mathrm{piecewise}}+n\cdot[D]\,\delta_S$ and $\operatorname{curl}H=\{\operatorname{curl}H\}_{\mathrm{piecewise}}+n\times[H]\,\delta_S$, with the analogous identities for $B$ and $E$. Substituting into the distributional identities of the hypothesis and using the sheet pairings of [[def-em-weak-sources]](c), the regular parts reproduce the off-interface macroscopic equations and the coefficients of $\delta_S$ give, one equation at a time, $n\cdot[D]=\sigma_f$ (from $\operatorname{div}D=\rho_f$), $n\cdot[B]=0$ (from $\operatorname{div}B=0$), $n\times[E]=0$ and $n\times[H]=K_f$: the right-hand sides $\partial_tB$ and $J_f+\partial_tD$ carry no delta term because $S$ is stationary and the joint one-sided $C^1$ hypothesis makes $\partial_tB$ and $\partial_tD$ locally bounded near $S$, hence locally integrable. Since the two-sided traces are continuous on $S\times I$, the distributional coefficient identities are the displayed pointwise identities. The weak-trace branch replaces the pointwise trace argument by the $dS\,dt$-almost-everywhere sheet identity plus the spatial-continuity upgrade. No constitutive relation and no field equation beyond the assumed distributional identities is used.

object.title: Energy balance and Ohmic dissipation for the constant nondispersive linear model
object.statement:
Assume the elementary inertial-rest branch of [[post-em-material-closure]]: constant symmetric positive-definite matrices $\varepsilon,\mu\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ (isotropic scalar case included) with $D=\varepsilon E$ and $B=\mu H$, and the conduction relation $J_f=\sigma E+J_{\mathrm{ext}}$ with $\sigma$ symmetric positive semidefinite and a declared external free current $J_{\mathrm{ext}}$. Assume the smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] with the regularity hypotheses of [[pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell]], so that its macroscopic equations hold on $\Omega\times I$. Define the stored-energy density and the energy-flux vector $$u:=\tfrac12\bigl(E\cdot D+B\cdot H\bigr),\qquad S:=E\times H,$$ with the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and the cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]; $u$ carries $\mathrm J\,\mathrm m^{-3}=\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^{-1}\mathrm s^{-2}$ and $S$ carries $\mathrm W\,\mathrm m^{-2}$. Then:
(a) [Local balance and positivity] On $\Omega\times I$, $$\partial_tu+\operatorname{div}S=-J_f\cdot E.$$ Moreover $u=\tfrac12(E\cdot\varepsilon E+H\cdot\mu H)\ge0$, with $u(x,t)>0$ whenever $(E(x,t),H(x,t))\ne(0,0)$.
(b) [Dissipation reading] With $J_f=\sigma E+J_{\mathrm{ext}}$ and $\sigma$ symmetric positive semidefinite, $E\cdot\sigma E\ge0$ and the balance reads $$\partial_tu+\operatorname{div}S+E\cdot\sigma E=-J_{\mathrm{ext}}\cdot E;$$ the nonnegative term $E\cdot\sigma E$ is the Ohmic dissipation density of the model.
(c) [Fixed-volume balance] Let $\Omega'\subseteq\Omega$ be open with $\overline{\Omega'}\subseteq\Omega$ carrying the finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation of [[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-piecewise-c-one-domains]], let $t_0<t_1$ with $(t_0,t_1)\subseteq I$, assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) as in that divergence theorem, and let $n$ be the outward unit normal of $\partial\Omega'$. Then for every $t\in(t_0,t_1)$, $$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega'}u(x,t)\,dx=-\int_{\Omega'}J_f\cdot E\,dx-\oint_{\partial\Omega'}S\cdot n\,dS.$$
(d) [Scope] The density $u=\tfrac12(E\cdot D+B\cdot H)$ is a stored-energy density only for this constant symmetric nondispersive model; for general dispersive, nonlocal, nonlinear or hysteretic response no instantaneous stored-energy density is defined or claimed by this item, and the general dispersive work balance is not supplied. The identities hold only where the fields and sources have the stated regularity, the fixed-volume form keeps its boundary term, and no conservation of $\int_{\Omega'}u$ is asserted unless that term vanishes. No empirical claim is made.
object.strategy: **Proof technique:** dot the macroscopic curl equations with the complementary fields and use the cross-product divergence identity. (a): by [[pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell]], $\operatorname{curl}H=J_f+\partial_tD$ and $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$. Taking the Euclidean inner product ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]) of the first with $E$ and of the second with $H$ gives $E\cdot\operatorname{curl}H=E\cdot J_f+E\cdot\partial_tD$ and $H\cdot\operatorname{curl}E=-H\cdot\partial_tB$. By [[lem-the-divergence-and-curl-of-a-cross-product]], $\operatorname{div}(E\times H)=H\cdot\operatorname{curl}E-E\cdot\operatorname{curl}H$; subtracting the two scalar equations from this identity gives $\operatorname{div}S+\partial_t\bigl(\tfrac12E\cdot D+\tfrac12B\cdot H\bigr)+J_f\cdot E=0$, because the symmetry of $\varepsilon$ gives $E\cdot\partial_tD=\tfrac12\partial_t(E\cdot\varepsilon E)$ and the symmetry of $\mu$ gives $H\cdot\partial_tB=\tfrac12\partial_t(H\cdot\mu H)$, using $D=\varepsilon E$, $B=\mu H$ and the product rule of [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]. Positivity is positive definiteness of $\varepsilon,\mu$: $u$ is a sum of two nonnegative quadratic forms, vanishing only when $E=H=0$. (b): $J_f\cdot E=E\cdot\sigma E+J_{\mathrm{ext}}\cdot E$ and $E\cdot\sigma E\ge0$ for symmetric positive semidefinite $\sigma$. (c): [[lem-em-parameter-integrals]] differentiates $t\mapsto\int_{\Omega'}u$ under the integral sign and [[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-piecewise-c-one-domains]] converts $\int_{\Omega'}\operatorname{div}S$ into the boundary flux; $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is exactly the hypothesis of that divergence theorem and is used only in this clause. (d) records the restrictions. No constitutive assumption beyond the declared closure branch, and no empirical premise, is used.

## Statement

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A set $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, functions $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ differentiable at $c$, and a real $\alpha$; for claim 4 also the hypothesis $g(c) \ne 0$ together with $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$ ([[def-derivative]], [[def-limit-point-r]]).

[L1] Carathéodory's characterisation ([[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]]), used in both directions: for a set $B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, a point $p \in B$ that is a limit point of $B$ and a function $h : B \to \mathbb{R}$, the function $h$ is differentiable at $p$ if and only if there is $\eta : B \to \mathbb{R}$, continuous at $p$, with $h(x) - h(p) = \eta(x)(x - p)$ for every $x \in B$, and then $\eta(p) = h'(p)$.

[L2] Algebra of continuous functions ([[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]]): sums, scalar multiples and products of functions continuous at a point are continuous there (claim 1); every constant function and the identity are continuous everywhere on the domain (claim 5); and if $u, v$ are continuous at a point $p$ of their common domain $D$ with $v(p) \ne 0$, then $p$ lies in $D_0 := \{x \in D : v(x) \ne 0\}$ and $(u/v)|_{D_0}$ is continuous at $p$ as a function on $D_0$ (claim 4).

[L3] Continuity passes to a subset of the domain: if $B \subseteq A$, if $p \in B$ and if $\psi : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous at $p$, then $\psi|_B$ is continuous at $p$, the condition on the restriction quantifying over fewer points ([[def-continuity-real]]).

[L4] A function differentiable at $c$ is continuous at $c$ ([[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]]); in particular $g$ is.

[L5] At a limit point $c$ of $A$, continuity of $g$ at $c$ says exactly that $\lim_{x \to c} g(x)$ exists and equals $g(c)$ ([[def-continuity-real]], clause 1, [[def-function-limit]]).

[L6] Sign preservation ([[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]]): if $c$ is a limit point of $A$ and $\lim_{x \to c} g(x)$ exists and is nonzero, then $c$ is a limit point of $A_0 = \{x \in A : g(x) \ne 0\}$.

[L7] A product of two nonzero reals is nonzero ([[lem-of-no-zero-divisors]]), and $g(c)^{2} = g(c)\,g(c)$ ([[def-integer-power]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [L1], applied to $f$ and to $g$ on $A$ at $c$, fix $\varphi, \psi : A \to \mathbb{R}$, both continuous at $c$, with $f(x) - f(c) = \varphi(x)(x - c)$ and $g(x) - g(c) = \psi(x)(x - c)$ for every $x \in A$, and with $\varphi(c) = f'(c)$ and $\psi(c) = g'(c)$. [L1, choose]

1.2 Assume $g(c) \ne 0$. Then $c \in A_0$ by the definition of $A_0$; $g$ is continuous at $c$ by [L4], so $\lim_{x \to c} g(x) = g(c) \ne 0$ by [L5]; and therefore $c$ is a limit point of $A_0$ by [L6]. [L4, L5, L6]

2.1 **Sum.** For every $x \in A$, $(f+g)(x) - (f+g)(c) = \bigl(f(x)-f(c)\bigr) + \bigl(g(x)-g(c)\bigr) = \bigl(\varphi(x) + \psi(x)\bigr)(x-c)$. The function $\varphi + \psi$ is continuous at $c$ by [L2], and $(\varphi+\psi)(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$. So [L1] gives claim 1. [step 1.1, L1, L2]

2.2 **Scalar multiple.** For every $x \in A$, $(\alpha f)(x) - (\alpha f)(c) = \alpha\bigl(f(x)-f(c)\bigr) = \bigl(\alpha\varphi(x)\bigr)(x-c)$. The function $\alpha\varphi$ is continuous at $c$ by [L2], with value $\alpha f'(c)$ there. So [L1] gives claim 2. [step 1.1, L1, L2]

2.3 **Product.** For every $x \in A$, $f(x)g(x) - f(c)g(c) = \bigl(f(x)-f(c)\bigr)g(x) + f(c)\bigl(g(x)-g(c)\bigr) = \bigl(\varphi(x)g(x) + f(c)\psi(x)\bigr)(x-c)$. Put $\chi := \varphi\,g + f(c)\,\psi$; it is continuous at $c$ by [L2], since $\varphi$, $\psi$ and (by [L4]) $g$ are, and constants are; and $\chi(c) = \varphi(c)g(c) + f(c)\psi(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$. So [L1] gives claim 3. [step 1.1, L1, L2, L4]

2.4 **Quotient, the rearrangement.** Assume $g(c) \ne 0$ and let $x \in A_0$, so $g(x) \ne 0$ and $g(c) \ne 0$. Then $f(x)/g(x) - f(c)/g(c) = \bigl(f(x)g(c) - f(c)g(x)\bigr)/\bigl(g(x)g(c)\bigr)$, and $f(x)g(c) - f(c)g(x) = \bigl(f(x)-f(c)\bigr)g(c) - f(c)\bigl(g(x)-g(c)\bigr) = \bigl(\varphi(x)g(c) - f(c)\psi(x)\bigr)(x-c)$. So, defining $\theta : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$ by $\theta(x) := \bigl(\varphi(x)g(c) - f(c)\psi(x)\bigr)/\bigl(g(x)g(c)\bigr)$, one has $(f/g)|_{A_0}(x) - (f/g)|_{A_0}(c) = \theta(x)(x-c)$ for every $x \in A_0$. [step 1.1, L1, L7]

2.5 **Quotient, continuity of the factor.** Assume $g(c) \ne 0$. The restrictions of $\varphi$, $\psi$ and $g$ to $A_0$ are continuous at $c \in A_0$ by [L3] and [L4], so by [L2] the numerator $u(x) := \varphi(x)g(c) - f(c)\psi(x)$ and the denominator $v(x) := g(x)g(c)$ are continuous at $c$ as functions on $A_0$. By [L7] the denominator vanishes at no point of $A_0$, so $\{x \in A_0 : v(x) \ne 0\} = A_0$, and $v(c) = g(c)^{2} \ne 0$; hence claim 4 of [L2] gives that $\theta = (u/v)|_{A_0}$ is continuous at $c$, with $\theta(c) = \bigl(\varphi(c)g(c) - f(c)\psi(c)\bigr)/g(c)^{2} = \bigl(f'(c)g(c) - f(c)g'(c)\bigr)/g(c)^{2}$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, L2, L3, L4, L7]

3.1 **Quotient, conclusion.** Assume $g(c) \ne 0$. By step 1.2 the point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$; by steps 2.4 and 2.5 the function $\theta : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous at $c$ and factors the increment of $(f/g)|_{A_0}$. So [L1], applied on the domain $A_0$ at the point $c$, gives that $(f/g)|_{A_0}$ is differentiable at $c$ with derivative $\theta(c)$: claim 4. [step 1.2, step 2.4, step 2.5, L1]

4.1 Claims 1 to 4 are proved, by steps 2.1, 2.2, 2.3 and 3.1 respectively, each by exhibiting the Carathéodory factor of the new function and reading its continuity at $c$ off the algebra of continuous functions. [step 2.1, step 2.2, step 2.3, step 3.1] ∎

## Remarks

- **The product rearrangement in one line.** The identity $fg - f(c)g(c) = (f - f(c))\,g + f(c)\,(g - g(c))$ splits the increment of a product into two increments, one multiplied by $g$ and one by a constant. It is the same identity that carries the product case of [[thm-algebra-of-function-limits]], read at the level of increments rather than of $\varepsilon$; here the factor $g$ has to be continuous at $c$ rather than merely bounded near it, and [[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]] is what supplies that.

- **The reciprocal is the case $f \equiv 1$.** Claim 4 then reads $\bigl((1/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) = -g'(c)/g(c)^{2}$, since $f'(c) = 0$ for a constant $f$; nothing separate has to be proved, and the derivative of a negative integer power on this page is obtained exactly this way.

- **Two hypotheses that look removable and are not.** In claim 4 the hypothesis $g(c) \ne 0$ cannot be weakened to "$g$ is nonzero somewhere near $c$", because $c$ itself must lie in the smaller domain for a derivative there to be a statement about $c$; and the conclusion is about $(f/g)|_{A_0}$, not about any extension of it to $A$, since no such extension is canonical.

## Statement

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The total first-order expansions of $f$ at $a$ and $g$ at $f(a)$.

[L1] In the total-derivative definition, the normalized remainder tends to zero as $h$ tends to zero ([[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]]).

[L2] Total differentiability gives a local $O(\|h\|_2)$ increment bound and therefore continuity ([[thm-total-differentiability-gives-a-local-linear-bound-and-continuity]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Write $f(a+h)=f(a)+Df(a)h+r_f(h)$ and $g(f(a)+k)=g(f(a))+Dg(f(a))k+r_g(k)$, with both normalized remainders tending to zero. [L1, L2]

2.1 By [L2], $k=f(a+h)-f(a)=O(\|h\|_2)$; boundedness of $Dg(f(a))$ and the two remainder limits show both $Dg(f(a))r_f(h)$ and $r_g(k)$ are $o(\|h\|_2)$, including the case $k=0$. [step 1.1, L2, algebra]

3.1 Substitution into the two expansions leaves $g(f(a+h))-g(f(a))-Dg(f(a))Df(a)h=o(\|h\|_2)$, and the composite of linear maps is linear. [step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Complex $z,w$ and real $x$.

[L1] [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]] says that the product has $n$th coefficient $\sum_{k\le n}a_kb_{n-k}$.

[L2] [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]] gives $\binom nk\,k!\,(n-k)!=n!$ for $k\le n$.

[L3] [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]] gives $(z+w)^n=\sum_{k\le n}\iota_{\mathbb C}\!\left(\binom nk\right)z^kw^{n-k}$, where $\iota_{\mathbb C}$ is its canonical-natural map.

[L4] [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]] states that $\sum z^n/n!$ converges absolutely for every complex $z$.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [L4], the two exponential series converge absolutely, so [L1] makes their product the Cauchy product. [L1, L4]

2.1 Its degree-$n$ coefficient is $\sum_{k\le n}z^kw^{n-k}/(k!(n-k)!)$. By [L2], after applying the canonical-natural map into $\mathbb C$, each summand is $\iota_{\mathbb C}\!\left(\binom nk\right)z^kw^{n-k}/n!$, and [L3] turns their sum into $(z+w)^n/n!$. [L2, L3, step 1.1]

3.1 The resulting series is the defining series of $\exp(z+w)$. When $z=x+0i$, every term is the corresponding real term in the definition of $e^x$, so the two values agree. [step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

The complex exponential is entire, and

$$ \exp'(z)=\exp z $$

for every $z\in\mathbb C$.

## Facts & Assumptions
**Given:** A complex number $z=x+iy$ and the published complex exponential.

[F1] For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ ([[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]).

[L1] The real exponential is $C^\infty$ and $(e^x)'=e^x$ ([[thm-derivative-of-exponential]]).

[L2] The real derivatives are $(\sin y)'=\cos y$ and $(\cos y)'=-\sin y$ ([[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]]).

[L3] A real function differentiable at a point is continuous there ([[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]]).

[L4] Finite sums and products of continuous real-valued maps on a topological space are continuous ([[lem-algebra-of-continuous-real-maps-on-a-space]]).

[L5] Continuous first partial derivatives satisfying the Cauchy–Riemann equations give complex differentiability, and holomorphy when this holds at every point ([[thm-continuous-partials-and-cauchy-riemann-imply-holomorphic]]). Where $f$ is complex differentiable, $f'=u_x+iv_x$ ([[thm-complex-differentiability-real-linearity-wirtinger-and-cauchy-riemann]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [F1], the real and imaginary components are $u(x,y)=e^x\cos y$ and $v(x,y)=e^x\sin y$. [given, F1]

2.1 By [L1] and [L2], $$u_x=e^x\cos y,\quad u_y=-e^x\sin y,\quad v_x=e^x\sin y,\quad v_y=e^x\cos y.$$ [step 1.1, L1, L2, algebra]

3.1 The one-variable factors in step 2.1 are continuous by [L1]–[L3]; their pullbacks along the coordinate projections are continuous, and [L4] makes all four displayed partials continuous on $\mathbb R^2$. [step 2.1, L1, L2, L3, L4]

4.1 Step 2.1 gives $u_x=v_y$ and $u_y=-v_x$ everywhere. By [L5], the complex exponential is entire and its derivative is $u_x+iv_x=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)=\exp z$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, L5] ∎

## Statement

$\mathbb C=\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)$ is a field containing the embedded copy of
$\mathbb R$. Every complex number has a unique form $a+bi$ with $a,b\in\mathbb R$,
and
$$ (a+bi)+(u+vi)=(a+u)+(b+v)i, $$
$$ (a+bi)(u+vi)=(au-bv)+(av+bu)i. $$
If $a+bi\ne0$, then
$$ (a+bi)^{-1}=\frac{a-bi}{a^2+b^2}. $$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The quotient construction $\mathbb C=\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)$.

[F1] The polynomial $x^2+1$ is irreducible over $\mathbb R$ ([[lem-x-squared-plus-one-is-irreducible-over-the-reals]]).

[F2] For a monic irreducible polynomial $p$ of degree $n$, $F[x]/(p)$ is a field extension of $F$ and every class has a unique representative of degree below $n$ ([[thm-irreducible-quotient-adjoins-a-root]]).

[F3] The real numbers form an ordered field ([[thm-reals-ordered-field]]).

[F4] In an ordered field every nonzero square is positive ([[lem-of-square-positive]]).

[F5] $\mathbb C$ is the quotient $\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)$ and $i=x+(x^2+1)$ ([[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Apply [F2] to [F1]. With the construction in [F5], this proves that $\mathbb C$ is a field, that the constant-class map embeds $\mathbb R$, and that every class has a unique representative $a+bx$, hence a unique form $a+bi$. [F1, F2, F5]

2.1 Quotient addition and multiplication, followed by $i^2=-1$, give the two displayed coordinate formulas. All field axioms are inherited from the field in step 1.1. [F5, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 If $a+bi\ne0$, uniqueness in step 1.1 gives $a\ne0$ or $b\ne0$. The corresponding square is positive by [F4], the other square is nonnegative, and therefore $a^2+b^2>0$ in the ordered field [F3]. [F3, F4, step 1.1]

3.1 Direct multiplication using step 2.1 gives $(a+bi)(a-bi)=a^2+b^2$. Since the real denominator is nonzero by step 2.2, division proves the inverse formula. [step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Every continuous real function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge1$, is Riemann integrable.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A continuous $f:Q\to\mathbb R$.

[L1] $Q$ is compact by Heine-Borel ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]], [[def-metric-compactness]]).

[L2] A continuous function on a compact metric space is uniformly continuous and bounded ([[thm-heine-cantor-metric]], [[thm-continuous-image-of-a-compact-space-is-compact]], [[thm-extreme-value-metric]], [[def-metric-continuity]]).

[L3] The Euclidean and sup-norm metrics are the published metrics and satisfy $d_2(x,y)\le\iota(m)d_\infty(x,y)$ ([[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]] clause 3, [[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]).

[L4] Arbitrarily small Darboux gaps characterize integrability ([[thm-multidimensional-riemann-criterion]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Given $\varepsilon>0$, use [L2] with oscillation target $\varepsilon/(1+\operatorname{vol}Q)$ and choose a grid whose mesh is below the resulting sup-metric radius.   [L1, L2, L3, given, choose]

2.1 Every cell then has oscillation below that target. Since cell volumes sum to $\operatorname{vol}Q$, the Darboux gap is below $\varepsilon$.   [step 1.1, given]

3.1 The multidimensional Riemann criterion proves integrability.   [step 2.1, L4] ∎

## Statement

Every $z=a+bi\in\mathbb C$ has a square root. If $b\ne0$, one square root is
$$u+vi,\qquad u=\sqrt{\frac{|z|+a}{2}},\qquad v=\frac{b}{2u}.$$
If $b=0$, one may take $\sqrt a$ when $a\ge0$, and
$i\sqrt{-a}$ when $a<0$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A complex number $z=a+bi$.

[F1] $|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$ ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]), and hence $|z|^2=a^2+b^2$ ([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]).

[F2] The real numbers are a complete ordered field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]), so every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

[F3] The real numbers form an ordered field ([[thm-reals-ordered-field]]).

[F4] Squaring is order-preserving and order-reflecting on nonnegative elements ([[lem-of-square-monotone]]).

[F5] Complex multiplication is $(a+bi)(u+vi)=(au-bv)+(av+bu)i$ ([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** cases.

1.1 Suppose $b=0$ and $a\ge0$. Then [F2] gives $(\sqrt a)^2=a=z$. [assume-case nonnegative, F2]

1.2 Suppose $b=0$ and $a<0$. Then [F2] gives $(i\sqrt{-a})^2=a=z$. [assume-case negative, F2, F3, algebra]

1.3 Suppose $b\ne0$. Then $b^2>0$, so [F1] gives $|z|^2>a^2$. If $a\ge0$, [F4] yields $|z|>a$; if $a<0$, it yields $|z|>-a$. In either case $|z|+a>0$. [assume-case nonzero, F1, F3, F4]

2.1 By [F2], $u=\sqrt{(|z|+a)/2}$ exists and is positive; hence $v=b/(2u)$ is defined. [F2, F3, step 1.3]

3.1 From $4u^2=2(|z|+a)$ and [F1], $$v^2=\frac{b^2}{4u^2} =\frac{|z|^2-a^2}{2(|z|+a)} =\frac{|z|-a}{2}.$$ [F1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Therefore $u^2-v^2=a$ and $2uv=b$, so coordinate multiplication gives $(u+vi)^2=a+bi=z$. [F5, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 The cases $b=0$ with $a\ge0$, $b=0$ with $a<0$, and $b\ne0$ are exhaustive, so every complex number has a square root. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 4.1, cases-exhaustive] ∎

## Statement

$$\exp(x)\to+\infty\quad(x\to+\infty),\qquad \exp(x)\to0\quad(x\to-\infty),$$
and the range of $\exp$ is contained in $(0,\infty)$ and is unbounded above with infimum $0$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The exponential series.

[L1] For $x\ge0$, every exponential-series term is nonnegative, so its sum dominates every partial sum and in particular $\exp(x)\ge1+x$ ([[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[thm-nonnegative-series-bounded-partial-sums]]).

[L2] $\exp(-x)=1/\exp(x)>0$ ([[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]]).

[L3] Finite and infinite limits of functions at infinity have the quantified definitions in [[def-limits-at-infinity]].

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Given a real $M$, every $x>\max\{0,M-1\}$ satisfies $\exp(x)\ge1+x>M$. Hence $\exp(x)\to+\infty$.  [L1, L3]

1.2 Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose $X>0$ with $1+X>1/\varepsilon$. If $x<-X$, then $-x>X$, so [L1] gives $\exp(-x)\ge1-x>1+X>1/\varepsilon$; [L2] yields $0<\exp(x)<\varepsilon$.  [L1, L2, choose]

2.1 The range assertions follow from positivity and the two limit conclusions.  [step 1.1, step 1.2, L2] ∎

## Statement

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Reals $a < b$, a function $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$, $f := G'$ integrable on $[a,b]$, and a partition $P = (n,t)$ of $[a,b]$.

[L1] For a partition $P = (n,t)$ of $[a,b]$: $t_0 = a$, $t_n = b$, $t_i < t_{i+1}$ for $i < n$, $\Delta_i = t_{i+1}-t_i > 0$, and $I_i = [t_i,t_{i+1}] \subseteq [a,b]$ ([[def-partition-and-refinement]], [[def-interval]]).

[L2] $L(f,P) = \sum_{i<n}m_i\Delta_i$ and $U(f,P) = \sum_{i<n}M_i\Delta_i$ with $m_i = \inf f[I_i]$ and $M_i = \sup f[I_i]$, so $m_i \le f(\xi) \le M_i$ for every $\xi \in I_i$ ([[def-darboux-sums]], [[def-bounded-set]]).

[L3] $\underline{\int_a^b} f = \sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\overline{\int_a^b} f = \inf_P U(f,P)$, and $f$ integrable means the two agree, their common value being $\int_a^b f$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

[L4] Mean value theorem: if $u$ is continuous on $[p,q]$ with $p<q$ and differentiable at every point of $(p,q)$, there is $\xi \in (p,q)$ with $u(q)-u(p) = u'(\xi)(q-p)$ ([[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).

[L5] A function differentiable at a point is continuous there, and the restriction of a differentiable function to a subinterval is differentiable with the same derivative at every point of that subinterval which is a limit point of it ([[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]], [[def-derivative]], [[def-continuity-real]]).

[L6] Finite sums: telescoping $\sum_{i<n}(c_{i+1}-c_i) = c_n - c_0$, and monotonicity in the terms ([[def-finite-sum]], [[lem-finite-sum-laws]], clauses 4 and 5).

[L7] Ordered-field arithmetic: multiplying an inequality by a positive real preserves it, the order is total and transitive, and a number that is an upper bound of a set and also a lower bound of another set lies between their supremum and infimum ([[def-ordered-field]], [[def-complete-ordered-field]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Let $P = (n,t)$ be an arbitrary partition of $[a,b]$ and let $i < n$. The restriction of $G$ to $I_i = [t_i,t_{i+1}]$ is continuous on $I_i$ and differentiable at every point of $(t_i,t_{i+1})$, with the same derivative $f$ there, by [L5] and [L1]. [given, L1, L5]

2.1 By [L4] applied on $I_i$ there is $\xi_i \in (t_i,t_{i+1})$ with $G(t_{i+1}) - G(t_i) = f(\xi_i)\,\Delta_i$; since $\xi_i \in I_i$ and $\Delta_i > 0$, [L2] gives $m_i\Delta_i \le G(t_{i+1})-G(t_i) \le M_i\Delta_i$. [step 1.1, L1, L2, L4, L7]

3.1 Step 2.1 holds for every $i < n$, so monotonicity of finite sums applies to the three families and gives $\sum_{i<n}m_i\Delta_i \le \sum_{i<n}\bigl(G(t_{i+1})-G(t_i)\bigr) \le \sum_{i<n}M_i\Delta_i$. [step 2.1, L6]

4.1 The middle sum telescopes to $G(t_n) - G(t_0) = G(b) - G(a)$ by [L6] and [L1], so $L(f,P) \le G(b)-G(a) \le U(f,P)$ by [L2]. [step 3.1, L1, L2, L6]

5.1 Step 4.1 holds for **every** partition $P$, so $G(b)-G(a)$ is an upper bound of the set of lower sums and a lower bound of the set of upper sums; hence $\underline{\int_a^b} f \le G(b)-G(a) \le \overline{\int_a^b} f$ by [L3] and [L7]. [step 4.1, L3, L7]

6.1 Since $f$ is integrable the two integrals coincide with $\int_a^b f$, so $\int_a^b f = G(b)-G(a)$. [step 5.1, L3] ∎

## Remarks

- **No choice principle is spent, and no sequence of tags is ever formed.** The usual proof selects one $\xi_i$ per subinterval and assembles the Riemann sum $\sum_i f(\xi_i)\Delta_i$, which is a choice from finitely many nonempty sets. The proof above never forms that family: step 2.1 proves, for an arbitrary fixed $i$, the *inequality* $m_i\Delta_i \le G(t_{i+1})-G(t_i) \le M_i\Delta_i$, which is a universally quantified statement about $i$ and needs no selection, and step 3.1 then sums the inequality. The telescoping identity supplies the middle term without any tags at all.

- **The hypothesis is differentiability at every point of the closed interval.** It is not enough to be differentiable on $(a,b)$ and continuous on $[a,b]$ in the argument as written, because step 2.1 uses the derivative only on open subintervals but the definition $f = G'$ has to name a function on all of $[a,b]$ for $\int_a^b f$ to mean anything. Changing $f$ at the two endpoints changes neither its integrability nor its integral ([[lem-changing-a-function-at-finitely-many-points]]), so the reader who prefers the weaker hypothesis loses nothing.

- **This is the half of the fundamental theorem that computes.** The other half, [[thm-ftc-first-part]], produces a primitive; this one evaluates an integral once a primitive is known, and it is the tool the companion page reaches for whenever a primitive is available. Where no primitive is at hand the companion page computes instead by splitting at a jump and using the integral of a constant; no claim is made here about how many of its computations take which route.

- **Forward references, orientation only.** The two witnesses showing neither hypothesis is removable are [[cex-a-function-with-a-primitive-that-is-not-integrable]] and [[cex-an-integrable-function-with-no-primitive]] on the companion page; nothing above depends on either.

## Statement

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A complete ordered field $F$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), that is, an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) with the least-upper-bound property, and an element $a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$.

[L1] Every nonempty subset of $F$ that is bounded above has a least upper bound in $F$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]).

[L2] Sign and scaling rules: a product of positives is positive, and for $c > 0$ one has $x < y \iff cx < cy$ ([[lem-of-sign-rules]]).

[L3] Squaring is strictly monotone on the nonnegatives: if $0 \le x < y$ then $x^2 < y^2$; in particular squaring is injective on $\{x : x \ge 0\}$ ([[lem-of-square-monotone]]).

[L4] A nonzero square is positive: if $y \neq 0$ then $y^2 > 0$ ([[lem-of-square-positive]]).

[L5] Multiplying inequalities of positives: if $0 < x < y$ and $0 < u < v$ then $xu < yv$ ([[prop-of-multiply-inequalities]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** contradiction.

1.1 If $a = 0$, then $s = 0$ satisfies $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = 0 = a$, so existence holds; assume henceforth $a > 0$. [given, algebra]

1.2 Uniqueness holds once a root exists: if $u, v \ge 0$ satisfy $u^2 = v^2$, then strict monotonicity of squaring on nonnegatives [L3] rules out both $u < v$ and $u > v$, forcing $u = v$; so at most one $s \ge 0$ has $s^2 = a$. [L3, given]

1.3 Define $S = \{ t \in F : t \ge 0 \text{ and } t^2 \le a \}$; then $0 \in S$ because $0 \ge 0$ and $0^2 = 0 \le a$, so $S \neq \emptyset$. [given, algebra]

1.4 The element $1 + a$ is an upper bound of $S$: since $a > 0$ we have $1 + a > 1$, so any $t > 1 + a$ has $t > 1$ and $t > 0$, whence $t^2 = t \cdot t > 1 \cdot t = t > 1 + a > a$, giving $t \notin S$. [given, L2]

2.1 By completeness [L1], $s := \sup S$ exists in $F$; and since $0 \in S$ we have $s \ge 0$. [L1, step 1.3, step 1.4]

3.1 Assume, for contradiction, that $s^2 \neq a$; by trichotomy either $s^2 < a$ or $s^2 > a$. [assume-contra, step 2.1]

4.1 (Case $s^2 < a$.) Choose $h$ with $0 < h < 1$ and $h < \dfrac{a - s^2}{2s + 1}$, possible since $a - s^2 > 0$ and $2s + 1 \ge 1 > 0$; then $h^2 = h \cdot h < h \cdot 1 = h$ and $h(2s+1) < a - s^2$, so $(s+h)^2 = s^2 + 2sh + h^2 < s^2 + 2sh + h = s^2 + h(2s+1) < a$, whence $s + h \in S$ with $s + h > s$, contradicting that $s$ is an upper bound of $S$. [assume-case low, step 3.1, step 2.1, L2, L5, choose]

4.2 (Case $s^2 > a$.) Here $s > 0$ since $s^2 > a \ge 0$; choose $h$ with $0 < h < s$ and $h < \dfrac{s^2 - a}{2s}$, so $2sh < s^2 - a$ and $(s-h)^2 = s^2 - 2sh + h^2 \ge s^2 - 2sh > a$, hence every $t \in S$ has $t^2 \le a < (s-h)^2$ with $t \ge 0$ and $s - h > 0$, so $t < s - h$ by [L3]; thus $s - h$ is an upper bound of $S$ with $s - h < s$, contradicting that $s$ is the least upper bound. [assume-case high, step 3.1, step 2.1, L3, choose]

5.1 Both cases of the disjunction in step 3.1 give a contradiction, so the assumption fails and $s^2 = a$: a unique (by step 1.2) $s = \sqrt{a} \ge 0$ with $s^2 = a$ exists, and applying this to any $x > 0$ writes $x = (\sqrt{x})^2$ with $\sqrt{x} \neq 0$ while conversely any nonzero square is positive by [L4], so the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the nonzero squares. [step 4.1, step 4.2, step 3.1, step 1.2, L4, cases, discharge-contradiction] ∎

## Statement

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sin(x+y)=\sin x\cos y+\cos x\sin y,$$
$$\cos(x+y)=\cos x\cos y-\sin x\sin y.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A fixed real $y$ and variable real $x$.

[L1] The harmonic-oscillator initial-value problem has the unique solution stated in [[thm-harmonic-oscillator-initial-value-characterization]].

[L2] Sine and cosine have the derivatives and values at zero of [[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]], and the chain rule applies ([[thm-chain-rule]]).



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The function $x\mapsto\sin(x+y)$ solves $u''=-u$ with initial values $u(0)=\sin y$, $u'(0)=\cos y$. [L2]

1.2 The function $x\mapsto\sin x\cos y+\cos x\sin y$ has the same equation and initial values. [L2, algebra]

2.1 Uniqueness in [L1] gives the sine addition formula. [step 1.1, step 1.2, L1]

3.1 Repeating the argument for $x\mapsto\cos(x+y)$ and $\cos x\cos y-\sin x\sin y$ gives the cosine addition formula. [L1, L2] ∎
